title: Delta Hedging a Vanilla Option
text: Delta hedging is the most fundamental risk management technique in options trading. By continuously adjusting a position in the underlying, a trader can eliminate first-order exposure to price movements.

title: Delta Hedging a Vanilla Option
text:
What is Delta?
The delta \(\Delta\) of an option measures the sensitivity of the option’s price to a small change in the underlying asset price:
\[\Delta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\]
For a European call under Black-Scholes, \(\Delta = N(d_1)\), where \(N(\cdot)\) is the standard normal CDF.

title: Delta Hedging a Vanilla Option
text:
Constructing the Hedge
To delta hedge a short call position, a trader buys \(\Delta\) shares of the underlying. As \(S\) moves, \(\Delta\) changes — so the hedge must be rebalanced continuously (in theory) or at discrete intervals (in practice).

title: Delta Hedging a Vanilla Option
text:
The Cost of Hedging
Rebalancing is not free. The P&L of a delta-hedged position depends on the difference between realised volatility and implied volatility — a key insight that connects hedging to volatility trading.

text:

title: Introduction to Options
text: Options are among the most versatile instruments in modern finance. This post introduces the key concepts needed to understand how options work before we get into pricing theory.

title: Introduction to Options
text:
What is an Option?
An option is a financial derivative that gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified price on or before a given date. The price paid for this right is called the premium.

title: Introduction to Options
text:
Calls and Puts
There are two fundamental types of options:

A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying at the strike price
A put option gives the holder the right to sell the underlying at the strike price

Each can be either bought (long) or sold (short), giving four basic positions.

title: Introduction to Options
text:
Key Terminology
Before diving into pricing, it helps to be precise about the core vocabulary: the strike price \(K\), the expiration date \(T\), the underlying price \(S_t\), and the risk-free rate \(r\). These four quantities appear in virtually every options model we will encounter.

title: Backtesting a Strategy
text: Backtesting is the process of simulating a trading strategy on historical data to evaluate its performance. Done carefully, it provides a useful signal about whether a strategy has merit — done carelessly, it produces misleading results.

title: Backtesting a Strategy
text:
The Basic Setup
A backtest requires three components: a signal (when to trade), a sizing rule (how much to trade), and a cost model (what execution costs). Getting all three right matters — an impressive backtest with no transaction costs tells you very little.

title: Backtesting a Strategy
text:
Common Pitfalls
The most dangerous backtesting mistakes are look-ahead bias (using future information that wouldn’t have been available at the time) and overfitting (tuning parameters until the in-sample performance looks good, at the expense of out-of-sample validity).

title: Backtesting a Strategy
text:
Evaluation Metrics
Raw return is a poor measure of strategy quality. Better metrics include the Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and the Calmar ratio — each capturing a different dimension of risk-adjusted performance.

title: Backtesting a Strategy
text:
References

title: Volatility Targeting
text: Volatility targeting is a position sizing technique that adjusts exposure inversely to realised volatility, keeping portfolio risk approximately constant through time.

title: Volatility Targeting
text:
The Core Idea
Rather than holding a fixed number of shares or a fixed notional position, a volatility-targeted strategy scales its position so that the expected portfolio volatility equals a target level \(\sigma^*\):
\[w_t = \frac{\sigma^*}{\hat{\sigma}_t}\]
where \(\hat{\sigma}_t\) is an estimate of current volatility, typically a rolling standard deviation of recent returns.

title: Volatility Targeting
text:
Why It Works
Volatility is mean-reverting and persistent. When markets are calm, vol targeting increases exposure; when markets are turbulent, it reduces it. This creates a natural mechanism for cutting risk during drawdowns — often before stop-losses would trigger.

title: Volatility Targeting
text:
Practical Considerations
The choice of lookback window for \(\hat{\sigma}_t\) matters significantly. Short windows are more responsive but noisier; long windows are more stable but lag regime changes. Transaction costs must also be weighed against the benefits of frequent rebalancing.

title: Volatility Targeting
text:
References


Hurst, Brian, Yao Hua Ooi, and Lasse Heje Pedersen. 2013. “Demystifying Managed Futures.” Journal of Investment Management 11 (3): 42–58.


Moreira, Alan, and Tyler Muir. 2017. “Volatility-Managed Portfolios.” Journal of Finance 72 (4): 1611–44.

title: Put-Call Parity
text: Put-call parity is one of the most elegant results in options theory. It establishes a precise relationship between the prices of European calls and puts on the same underlying, with the same strike and expiration.

title: Put-Call Parity
text:
The Relationship
For European options on a non-dividend-paying stock, put-call parity states:
\[C - P = S_0 - K e^{-rT}\]
where \(C\) is the call price, \(P\) is the put price, \(S_0\) is the current stock price, \(K\) is the strike, \(r\) is the risk-free rate, and \(T\) is the time to expiration.

title: Put-Call Parity
text:
Deriving it from No-Arbitrage
The relationship follows directly from the no-arbitrage principle. Consider two portfolios: one holding a call and a bond, the other holding a put and the stock. Both portfolios have identical payoffs at expiration — so by no-arbitrage, they must have the same value today.

title: Put-Call Parity
text:
Implications
Put-call parity is model-free — it holds regardless of how we model the underlying. This makes it a powerful tool for detecting mispricing and for synthesising positions synthetically.

title: Put-Call Parity
text:
References


Hull, John C. 2018. Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives. 10th ed. Pearson.


Merton, Robert C. 1973. “Theory of Rational Option Pricing.” The Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 4 (1): 141–83.
